newsitem.title: USA: Safeway bids for Vons in $2.3 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: Safeway bids for Vons in $2.3 billion deal.

text.p: Safeway Inc. Wednesday offered to buy the rest of supermarket chain Vons Cos. Inc. in a $2.3 billion deal that would create the second-biggest grocery store chain in the country.
The offer points to further consolidation in the hotly competitive industry, after Dutch supermarket company Ahold NV recent took over the Massachusetts-based Stop & Shop chain.
Merger and acquisition experts said a friendly deal was likely since Safeway already owns about a third of Vons' stock and the companies share common directors.

"My guess is it's friendly," one merger specialist said. "There are a lot of overlapping board members and there's (Safeway's) ownership of (Vons) stock. From a fairness standpoint, Safeway had to make it look favourable for Vons."
Vons said a committee of its outside directors would study Safeway's offer and respond "in due course."

California-based Safeway, which operates 1,050 stores in the United States and Canada, already owns 34.5 percent of Vons, which operates 325 stores, mostly in southern California, under the Vons and Pavilions names.

The combination of Safeway and Vons would create the second-largest grocery store chain in North America, with 1,375 stores operating in 16 states, the District of Columbia and five Canadian provinces and sales in excess of $22.5 billion, Safeway said.

The nation's largest supermarket chain is Kroger Co. But the proposed combination will be most problematic for key competitors of Safeway and Vons, including Albertson's Inc., Ralphs Grocery Co. and Giant Food Inc.

"The combination will make for a western powerhouse without equal. It's very exciting for Safeway holders in the longer term and it's a fair price," said Mark Husson, analyst with J.P. Morgan Securities.
Industry experts said investment firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co., which owns 52 percent of Safeway, has thrown its support behind the deal.

KKR is the linchpin linking the company's boards. Robert MacDonnell is a KKR general partner and director of both Safeway and Vons, and KKR executive James Greene is a director of both. In addition, they said, Safeway Chairman Peter Magowan and President Steve Burd also sit on both boards.
In a letter to Vons, Safeway offered to exchange 1.34 Safeway shares for each Vons share not owned by Safeway.

Based on Safeway's price of $43.375 a share on Tuesday, the deal would value Vons shares at about $58 apiece, giving the stock portion of the deal a value of $1.68 billion. In addition, Safeway would assume about $550 million in debt, bringing the total value to around $2.3 billion.
Vons jumped $11.25 to $54.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Despite the companies' strong links, Burd noted there were no overlaps among the two store chains.

"We have virtually no overlap with Vons at this time and so there are no redundant facilities to worry about having to close," Burd said. "You shouldnt get the impression that being more efficient leads to a job loss, quite the contrary."

Safeway has cut costs aggressively to make itself into a tough competitor after being seen as a slow-footed chain a decade ago. In 1986, Safeway received an unsolicited takeover bid from the Dart Group. In response, Magowan and KKR took Safeway private in a buyout. Safeway sold some 1,200 locations in 1987 and 1988 including stores in southern California to Vons for 35 percent of Vons stock.
In 1990, Safeway re-emerged as a public company.
For its last fiscal year, Safeway reported net income of $111.9 million, or $1.34 a share, on revenues of $5.17 billion.
Analysts said the merger should fuel Safeway's growth.
"Safeway management was running out of opportunities to upgrade its profitability and now it's got a new field to plough," said Jonathan Ziegler, analyst with Salomon Brothers.
Safeway's Burd said he expects a "smooth transaction" with Vons and thought it was reasonable to believe this could be completed early next year or by spring.
